paragraphs.text: This basket tea was made in 1985 in [Qimen County](qimen:where-it-is), in the hills of southern Anhui near the Huangshan mountains. It comes from the local small leaf bush that also gives [Keemun](qimen:known-for). The name points elsewhere: [Lu'an](anhui:lu-an-names) is a city in western Anhui known for a green tea, while this tea takes its name from the old Liu An way of making and trading.

[Liu An](liu-an:definition) is a [dark tea](dark:definition), so the leaf keeps changing slowly after it is made. Spring leaf is first made much like a green tea, then fired over charcoal in autumn and spread outdoors for one night to take the [night dew](liu-an:making). It is steamed soft, packed into small [bamboo baskets](liu-an:basket) lined with bamboo leaf and fired once more. It is sold only after it has rested for some years.

At forty-one years, this basket has rested far longer than the usual three. The style is said to [improve with years in its basket](liu-an:ageing), as long as it is kept dry and in wrapping that breathes. Basket tea was mostly known through the [southern trade](liu-an:southern-trade) in Guangdong, Hong Kong and Macau, where people kept it at home and in medicine shops.

brewing.text: Use water at or near the boil, rinse the leaf quickly, and keep the steeps short, each a little longer than the last, in a gaiwan or clay pot; doses run from about 3 to 8 grams for 100 ml, for six to ten or more steeps. A small piece of the basket's bamboo leaf is often brewed with it. Aged tea can also be simmered in a larger pot, about 1 gram to 200 to 300 ml, for a few minutes or longer.

notice.text: A redder, browner liquor, the smoke gone, and the cup moving toward medicinal, woody and camphor notes, often with betel nut.
